A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same distributional-unlearning framework, algorithms, theory, and core experiments despite the changed title. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic Gaussian experiments and evaluations on Jigsaw Toxic Comments, SMS Spam, and CIFAR-10, including supplementary results in Appendix B.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds selection comparisons combined with sample-level unlearning methods in Section 4.3 and Table 5.

M1.justification: The distance-to-retained-mean scoring, top-f deletion, and Gaussian MLE steps remain unchanged, as do the cosine, Mahalanobis, and likelihood-ratio heuristics. Section 4.3 evaluates the existing selectors with established downstream unlearning methods without introducing a new proposed selection component.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Gaussian configurations, Jigsaw profanity-defined subpopulation, SMS spam-versus-ham task, and CIFAR-10 cat-versus-other-classes task. Table 5 reuses Gaussian and CIFAR-10 coverage. Describing CIFAR-10 and Jigsaw as well-separated and intertwined scenarios reframes existing experiments; SMS moves to the appendix.

E2.justification: Table 5 adds centroid-based Coreset comparisons, and Section 4.3 reports evaluating k-center greedy with near-identical performance. The new comparison matrix evaluates Random, Coreset, and Selective selection with retraining, finetuning, NegGrad+, and SalUn on CIFAR-10, and retraining versus influence-function updates on Gaussians. These comparisons were absent from v1.

E3.justification: Table 5 introduces evaluation across downstream unlearning procedures, including a 20% CIFAR-10 forget-class accuracy target and method-specific training budgets documented in Appendix B.2.2. Table 2 also changes the savings metric from reduction relative to random deletion to reduction relative to full removal. Existing dataset splits remain unchanged. Jigsaw preservation is relabeled from macro-F1 to F1 without specifying whether averaging changed.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 adds a substantial analysis of whether selection benefits persist across approximate unlearning procedures, extending validation beyond retraining. It also tests forget-set representativeness through coreset selection. The existing Gaussian separation sweep and Figure 6 comparison of scoring heuristics are retained.

E5.justification: The documented counts remain 20 Gaussian, five Jigsaw, ten SMS, and thirty CIFAR-10 seeds. Existing mean and standard-error reporting is retained. Table 5 adds deletion-budget point estimates but introduces no new uncertainty-estimation practice or explicitly increased run count.

E6.justification: Table 5 adds results without counterparts in v1: for example, CIFAR-10 Selective versus Random deletion budgets are 70% versus 88% with NegGrad+ and 55% versus 68% with SalUn; Gaussian influence-function budgets are 18% versus 91%. Original Table 2 deletion budgets and matched performance curves are retained. Savings changes such as 72% to 82% reflect the changed denominator, not improved same-setting performance.

T1.justification: The central definitions, frontier formulas, log-loss bounds, and Appendix A proofs are retained; v1's exponential-family Proposition 3 becomes v3's Theorem 2. Limited refinements include explicitly specifying positive shared covariance and removing v1 Section 3.2's reversed assignment of square-root and fourth-root deletion bounds, while retaining Table 1's original formulas.

C1.justification: v3 recasts the main efficiency contribution around reducing the forget set for computationally expensive sample-level unlearning and adds an explicit claim of compatibility with several such methods. The headline empirical claim changes from 15–72% savings versus random deletion to 15–82% versus full removal. This redefines the principal efficiency comparison while retaining the underlying KL framework.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning Gaussian finite-sample guarantees, dependence on upstream domain identification, and the absence of privacy-oriented evaluation. Sections 4.2–4.3 develop interpretations based on concentrated statistical influence and explain coreset performance through ignoring retained data. Remarks 9–10 discuss the relationship between deletion budgets, downstream computation, and selection overhead, replacing much of v1's speculative concluding discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2.2 newly documents optimizers, learning rates, epochs, batch sizes, SalUn's saliency fraction, NegGrad+ weighting, and influence-function damping. Appendix B.2.1 adds coreset implementation descriptions. v3 also replaces ResNet feature references with CNN terminology consistent with v1's detailed CIFAR-10 procedure. Existing dataset-processing and hardware disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts toward complementing computational unlearning methods and contrasting two-distribution selection with conventional coresets. New citations include Mirzasoleiman et al. and Gentile et al. for coresets, Fan et al. for SalUn, and Eldan and Russinovich for domain unlearning. The earlier distributionally robust optimization and spurious-feature-pruning discussion is removed, while the coreset relationship receives substantive new argument and empirical support.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, methodological explanations, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized around CIFAR-10 and Jigsaw case studies followed by the new synergy section; SMS moves to Appendix B.1. Appendix B gains a nested structure separating additional results from implementation details.

P2.justification: The document adopts substantially different typography, heading styles, margins, and page rules, with resized and repositioned displays. The CIFAR-10 plot moves from v1's appendix Figure 5 to main-text Figure 3, alongside Jigsaw Figure 4. Other figures are relocated, and a new two-part Table 5 is added. Existing plotted curves are preserved.

improvement.justification: Table 5 broadens empirical support beyond retraining, while the added implementation details and explicit Gaussian, domain-identification, and privacy-evaluation limitations improve clarity and scope calibration. The gain is limited: the larger headline savings reexpress unchanged deletion budgets, and Appendix B.2.2 describes retraining as using only p2 despite Table 5 varying partial-deletion budgets, leaving an important ambiguity in reproducing the new comparisons.
